summary: Defines BGP-4, an inter-autonomous system routing protocol for the Internet. It was a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 1771.

eli5.summary: Different networks need a way to tell each other which paths lead where. This is an early description of the protocol that does that. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how does border gateway protocol work
subtitle: The protocol that lets different autonomous systems exchange routing information across the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet is not a single network but a collection of independently managed networks (autonomous systems). Each needs to know how to reach networks in other systems. Earlier protocols like EGP did not scale well or support the policies needed for modern interdomain routing.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-4 establishes TCP connections between border routers in different autonomous systems, exchanges routing information as UPDATE messages describing reachable network prefixes and the path of AS numbers to reach them, and applies local policies to decide which routes to use and advertise. It uses KEEPALIVE messages to maintain connections and NOTIFICATION messages to signal errors.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 remains the de facto standard for Internet routing, though it was refined by RFC 1771 and later updated again. It introduced support for classless addressing (CIDR) and route aggregation, which made interdomain routing more scalable.

today: RFC 1654 was superseded by RFC 1771, also titled "A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)", which incorporated updates from operational experience. BGP-4 remains the Internet's primary interdomain routing protocol.

sections.title: Inter-Autonomous System Routing
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol. An autonomous system (AS) is a set of routers under a single technical administration that run an internal routing protocol and present themselves as a single entity to the outside world. BGP allows these systems to exchange reachability information: which networks can be reached through which paths.

BGP-4 adds support for classless interdomain routing (CIDR), representing networks as IP prefixes (e.g., 192.0.2.0/24) rather than class-based networks. It also supports route aggregation, allowing multiple routes to be summarized into a single, less-specific prefix. These features made the Internet's routing tables more manageable as the number of networks grew.
sections.eli5: Routers at the edge of different networks connect to each other and tell each other how to reach the networks they serve.

sections.title: How BGP Peers Communicate
sections.content:
Two BGP speakers establish a TCP connection (port 179) and exchange OPEN messages to negotiate parameters like hold time (how long to wait for messages before timing out) and each speaker's AS number. The initial exchange transmits the entire routing table. After that, UPDATE messages carry incremental changes as routes become available or are withdrawn.

KeepAlive messages are sent periodically to ensure the connection stays alive. If an error occurs, a NOTIFICATION message is sent with an error code, and the connection is closed. BGP does not require periodic refresh of the entire routing table; the local BGP speaker is responsible for maintaining the current state of routes learned from peers.
sections.eli5: Two routers connect via TCP, exchange their full route list, then send updates whenever routes change. Periodic heartbeat messages keep the connection alive.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
All BGP messages begin with a 19-octet header: a 16-octet Marker field (used for authentication and synchronization), a 2-octet Length field, and a 1-octet Type field (OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, or NOTIFICATION).

OPEN messages include the protocol version (currently 4), the sender's AS number, proposed hold time, BGP identifier (an IP address), and optional authentication data. UPDATE messages specify prefixes to be withdrawn, path attributes describing the route (origin, AS path, next hop, and optional attributes like local preference), and new reachability information. KEEPALIVE messages are just the header (19 octets). NOTIFICATION messages carry an error code and subcode describing what went wrong.
sections.eli5: Messages have a header naming the type (OPEN, UPDATE, etc.), and the body varies: OPEN includes the router's AS number, UPDATE lists prefixes and how to reach them, KEEPALIVE is just a heartbeat.

sections.title: Path Attributes and Routing Policies
sections.content:
Each advertised route carries path attributes that describe how to reach the destination and what policies apply. Mandatory attributes that every route must have include ORIGIN (whether the route came from the local AS, via EGP, or by some other means), AS_PATH (the ordered list of AS numbers the route has traversed), and NEXT_HOP (the IP address of the border router to use as the next hop).

Optional attributes include MULTI_EXIT_DISC (a metric for choosing among multiple exit points to the same AS), LOCAL_PREF (a preference value for internal routing), ATOMIC_AGGREGATE (indicating that a less-specific route was chosen), and AGGREGATOR (recording which AS performed aggregation). Path attributes are organized into three routing information bases: Adj-RIBs-In (received routes), Loc-RIB (routes the local system will use), and Adj-RIBs-Out (routes to advertise to peers).
sections.eli5: Each route comes with tags: where it originated, which AS systems it has passed through, and the next router to use. There are also optional tags for preferences and policies.

sections.title: Connection States and Finite State Machine
sections.content:
BGP connection establishment follows a finite state machine with six states: Idle (waiting to start), Connect (waiting for TCP to succeed), Active (trying to connect), OpenSent (sent OPEN, waiting for peer's OPEN), OpenConfirm (peer's OPEN accepted, waiting for KEEPALIVE), and Established (ready to exchange routes).

In Idle state, no resources are allocated. When a Start event occurs, the system initializes resources, starts a retry timer, and moves to Connect. If TCP succeeds, an OPEN message is sent and the state becomes OpenSent. The peer responds with KEEPALIVE to confirm, moving to OpenConfirm. Once both sides send KEEPALIVE, the state becomes Established and routes can be exchanged. If an error occurs at any point, the system sends NOTIFICATION and returns to Idle, with exponential backoff (60 seconds initially, doubled on each retry) before attempting to reconnect.
sections.eli5: Routers start in an idle state, try to connect, exchange OPEN messages to agree on parameters, and once both confirm with KEEPALIVE, they start exchanging routes.

sections.title: Error Detection and Reporting
sections.content:
NOTIFICATION messages report six classes of errors: Message Header errors (bad length or type), OPEN errors (unsupported version, bad peer AS, bad BGP identifier, unsupported authentication), UPDATE errors (malformed attributes, missing mandatory attributes, invalid ORIGIN or NEXT_HOP, AS routing loops), Hold Timer expired, Finite State Machine errors, and Cease (graceful shutdown).

When processing an UPDATE message, the receiver checks path attributes for correctness and consistency. If an optional transitive attribute is unrecognized, the route is accepted and the attribute is passed along with the Partial bit set. Unrecognized non-transitive attributes are silently dropped. This mechanism allows new attributes to be introduced without breaking older implementations.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, a NOTIFICATION message says what the problem is: bad format, missing field, loop detected, or connection timeout.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total message length in octets (19 to 4096).

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type: OPEN (1), UPDATE (2), NOTIFICATION (3), KEEPALIVE (4).
